prompt.context: Our client is a national chain of movie theaters. They have come to us concerned that they are not doing as well as they used to.
prompt.question: What do you recommend they do?

clarifying_info.q: Are they down in revenue, profitability, or both?
clarifying_info.a: They are down in both revenue and profitability.
Revenue sources are: Tickets, Concessions, and Other (which includes theater rentals and advertising).

clarifying_info.q: Has the number of movies being released or watched declined?
clarifying_info.a: Movies being seen have not declined overall, but there is a shift to online viewing over attendance at the theater.

framework: Revenue analysis: break into Ticket Sales, Concessions, and Other; identify which streams are growing or shrinking
Cost analysis: examine major cost buckets (Film Rental, Staff, Concession, Facilities) and assess how their composition has shifted
Market/customer analysis: assess volume trends (tickets sold) and customer segmentation (frequency of attendance)
Competitive/industry context: understand shift from theatrical viewing to online/streaming distribution
Recommendation: synthesize findings into actionable levers across revenue, cost, and customer retention

questions.prompt: Question 1 – Exhibit 1 insights: After the candidate builds a revenue framework, present Exhibit 1. What do you observe?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify that Ticket Sales are the largest revenue source and have been declining since roughly 2007. Concessions are actually trending upward, suggesting higher spend per customer (either price increases or higher volume per visit). Candidate should proactively ask about the 'Other' category and brainstorm its components (advertising revenue from pre-film commercials, parking revenue, theater rentals for events). Strong candidates note that relying on a declining core revenue stream while concessions offset only partially is unsustainable.

math.setup: Approximate ticket price increase: Ticket revenue in 2002 ~$10,354MM; Ticket revenue in 2014 ~$9,099MM. Tickets sold declined (see Exhibit 3). Combining both, ticket prices have risen roughly 40% to partially offset volume loss.
steps: From Exhibit 3, ticket volume declined significantly from 2002 to 2014
Ticket revenue fell only modestly (~12%) despite the volume decline
Implied average ticket price increased ~40% over the period to sustain revenues on lower volume
math.answer: Ticket prices rose ~40% from 2002 to 2014 as the chain tried to offset falling attendance with higher prices per ticket.

questions.prompt: Question 2 – Exhibit 2 insights: Once costs are discussed, present Exhibit 2. What do you observe, and why might film rental costs be rising?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize that Film Rental is now a significantly larger share of total costs in 2014 vs 2002 (grew from ~$5,802MM to ~$8,236MM in absolute terms, and as a share of total costs). The follow-up question is: why would film rental prices be increasing? A strong candidate should brainstorm that movie studios now have many more distribution options (iTunes, Netflix, streaming platforms) beyond theaters and DVD, giving them higher negotiating leverage. Studios can extract higher rental fees from theaters because theaters have fewer substitutes as distribution channels, while studios can achieve comparable or better margins through digital channels with lower distribution costs.

steps: Film rental grew both in absolute terms (+$2,434MM) and as a share of costs (+6.4 pp)
math.answer: Film rental costs grew from ~49% to ~55% of total costs, driven by studios gaining leverage through digital distribution alternatives.

questions.prompt: Question 3 – Exhibits 3 and 4 insights: Present Exhibits 3 and 4. What do you observe, and what can the client do?
questions.guidance: From Exhibit 3, the number of tickets sold is falling steadily, confirming volume erosion. Combined with the ~40% ticket price increase inferred from Exhibit 1 + 3, it is likely unsustainable to maintain revenues purely by raising prices on a shrinking customer base. From Exhibit 4, the most valuable customers (frequent moviegoers, 4+ movies/month) declined sharply from 27% to 9% of the base. This is a significant loss of high-value, repeat customers. Strong candidates should suggest loyalty programs or unlimited monthly passes to retain and re-engage frequent moviegoers, since these customers have the highest lifetime value and are most at risk of substituting to streaming.

A strong recommendation covers: (1) Acknowledge the structural trend — shift to online viewing is reducing attendance and ticket volume, which cannot be fully offset by raising prices; (2) Cost pressure — film rental costs are rising as studios gain leverage via digital channels, squeezing margins further; (3) Customer retention — the most frequent moviegoers (highest LTV segment) are being lost at an accelerating rate; propose loyalty/rewards programs or monthly unlimited passes to re-engage them; (4) Revenue diversification — pursue alternative revenue streams such as theater rentals for corporate events/private screenings, expanding advertising revenue, and enhancing the premium in-theater experience (premium formats, food/beverage upgrades) to differentiate from home viewing; (5) Concession opportunity — concession revenue is growing, suggesting customers who do attend are spending more; investing in premium food/beverage could amplify this trend.

brainstorming.prompt: Why might film rental costs be increasing? What are possible reasons movie studios can charge theaters more?

categories.name: Studio leverage via new distribution channels
ideas: iTunes and other digital download platforms give studios direct-to-consumer revenue
Netflix and streaming services offer studios new licensing revenue streams with leaner cost structures
Studios can release films simultaneously or quickly on digital platforms, reducing dependence on theatrical windows
Fewer middlemen in digital distribution means higher margins for studios, raising their outside option

categories.name: Consolidation or market power
ideas: If major studios have consolidated, their bargaining power over theater chains increases
Blockbuster tentpole films are scarce and theaters must bid competitively to secure them

categories.name: Declining theater attendance reducing studio incentive to subsidize theaters
ideas: As theatrical attendance falls, studios have less reason to offer favorable rental terms
Theaters are a less attractive distribution partner relative to growing digital platforms

categories.name: Other revenue streams for theaters
ideas: Renting theaters out for private events, corporate screenings, gaming tournaments
Expanded food and beverage or full dining experiences

recommendation: The client faces a structural profitability challenge driven by falling ticket volumes, rising film rental costs from studio leverage, and the accelerating loss of high-frequency customers to streaming alternatives.

Priority actions: launch a loyalty or unlimited monthly pass program to re-engage frequent moviegoers; pursue aggressive theater-rental and event-hosting revenue to diversify away from ticket dependency; invest in premium in-theater experiences (food, premium formats) to create differentiation from home streaming that justifies higher ticket prices sustainably.
risks: Continued erosion of attendance if streaming penetration deepens further
Studios may continue raising rental fees, compressing margins even if revenue is stabilized
Unlimited pass programs may cannibalize per-ticket revenue if pricing is set too aggressively
Premium experience investments require capital and may not generate sufficient ROI if volume does not recover
next_steps: Pilot a monthly unlimited moviegoing pass in selected markets and measure impact on visit frequency and total revenue per member
Conduct a detailed analysis of theater rental market opportunity (corporate, private events) and identify venues suitable for conversion
Negotiate with studios for multi-year rental agreements to lock in cost certainty
Evaluate premium format upgrades (IMAX, Dolby) to increase average ticket value and create a defensible experiential moat against streaming
